description: We're a team passionate about space exploration, science, and innovation. We aim to combine our skills to develop creative, practical solutions to real-world challenges using NASA data. We're looking for motivated participants with diverse skills in physics, programming, data analysis, astronomy, and design who enjoy teamwork and learning together.
summary:
HOMEBOUND is an interactive Mars survival game. You play as the first astronaut on Mars, with a rover named DUNE as your only companion on the surface. You explore the terrain around your habitat, manage limited supplies, and receive delayed messages from Mission Control on Earth.

The game asks players to weigh competing needs: how much oxygen to spend exploring, which systems to keep powered, and when to turn back. NASA research on Earth–Mars communications and crop experiments aboard the International Space Station informs the game’s transmissions and greenhouse.

HOMEBOUND lets players experience why astronauts protect their reserves, plan for the return trip, and make decisions on their own when help from Earth takes time.
details:
What we built

HOMEBOUND is a browser-based Mars survival game. The player is the first astronaut on Mars, with a rover named DUNE as their only companion on the surface. Players explore around their habitat, collect materials, check their inventory, and give DUNE commands such as Follow me, Wait here, and Go to base. In the server room, they can read delayed transmissions from Mission Control on Earth.

How it works

The game combines open exploration with decisions about limited resources. In First Night, the player weighs whether to spend suit oxygen searching for a spare power module or stay at the habitat and reduce electricity use. Recovering the module can keep more systems running overnight. Staying inside avoids the risks of the trip, but may mean turning off the greenhouse lights to keep life support powered. The player learns by seeing what their plan costs and what it keeps running.

What makes it creative

We wanted Mars to feel worth exploring and the habitat to feel worth returning to. Outside, terrain and equipment give the player clues to follow. Inside, those discoveries become decisions about what to repair, power, or postpone. DUNE adds personality through short exchanges and gives the player company without making every trip an escort mission.

Research and design considerations

NASA’s Mars Relay Network informed how we handle communication with Earth. The delay explains why the player sometimes has to act before Mission Control can respond. NASA crop experiments aboard the International Space Station informed the greenhouse’s crop selection and lighting details. We used those sources as references and chose gameplay values for oxygen and power so players can read the trade-offs before committing. Our goal is to help players understand why an astronaut must plan the return trip, protect reserves, and make decisions locally.

Development tools

We used Codex to assist with implementation and iteration, and published the browser build on Netlify.
